oa_title: Power imbalance between digital labour platforms and platform workers
abstract: The legal debate on platform work is largely dominated by the labour-law question: to be or not to be an employee. This dissertation looks at platform work from the perspective of European competition law. Central to this are self-employed platform workers, who are in principle considered undertakings under competition law. The central research question is: How can EU competition law respond to power imbalances in the relationship between digital labour platforms and platform workers? The dissertation combines doctrinal legal research with interdisciplinary and normative analysis. The main research question is approached through a framework consisting of three pathways. The first pathway focuses on worker empowerment. The EU aims to strengthen the position of platform workers in two ways. On the one hand, there is the Platform Work Directive (2024), which aims to correctly classify falsely self-employed workers as employees. On the other hand, there are the European Commission’s Collective Bargaining Guidelines (2022), which aim to create room for certain self-employed workers to bargain collectively without competition law forming a barrier. This can lead to countervailing power, thereby reducing workers’ dependency. The dissertation also describes the limitations of this pathway: reclassification is partly left to the Member States and the Guidelines are non-binding.
